item.title: Reconstructing Glacier Dynamics in Complex Terrain with ICESat-2 and Gaussian Process Interpolation
item.dc:creator: Thorsten Seehaus, Alex S. Gardner, Johan Nilsson
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: glacier, Antarctica, sea level, sea-level rise
Satellite altimeters only sample surface heights at scattered points. We developed a method to turn these measurements into maps of glacier height change while also estimating how reliable the results are. Applying this approach to glaciers in Svalbard and Antarctica shows strong ice loss and clearly captures short-lived events such as glacier surges. Our results improve the ability to monitor glacier change in difficult terrain and help better assess future contributions to sea level rise.

item.title: Stratospheric aerosol forcing for CMIP7 – Part 2: Volcanic sulfur dioxide emissions
item.dc:creator: Thomas J. Aubry, Michael Sigl, Matthew Toohey, Man Mei Chim, Magali Verkerk, Anja Schmidt, … (+1)
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development — matched: model intercomparison, CMIP
We document the historical (1750–2023) volcanic sulfur dioxide emission dataset created for phase 7 of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project, which is a set of coordinated climate model experiments run by modelling center worldwide. Our dataset underpins the stratospheric aerosol optical property dataset which will be used as input by most climate models. However, models with interactive stratospheric aerosol capability can directly input our emission dataset to run CMIP7 experiments.

item.title: Covariance-Informed Ensemble Score Filtering: Embedding Localized Covariance Geometry into Score-Based Transport
item.dc:creator: Siming Liang, Peter Jan van Leeuwen, Hristo G. Chipilski, Zezhong Zhang, Feng Bao, Guannan Zhang
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: data assimilation, ensemble
arXiv:2610.32148v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Background-error covariance models are central to atmospheric data assimilation because they spread partial observational information across space, variables, and dynamically coupled scales. Ensemble and variational methods exploit this covariance geometry efficiently, but their standard analysis formulations are largely built around Gaussian or locally quadratic approximations. Score-based ensemble filtering provides a framework for nonlinear distributional transport, but existing Ensemble Score Filter (EnSF) formulations lack an intrinsic covariance-mediated pathway for propagating likelihood information from observed to unobserved state components. We introduce a covariance-informed ensemble score filter (CI-EnSF) that embeds localized forecast-error covariance geometry directly into the forward diffusion and reverse transport. The proposed forward diffusion is covariance-shaped in standardized state space and becomes isotropic under the corresponding control-variable transformation. This covariance structure continuously propagates observational information from observed to unobserved state components throughout the reverse transport analysis trajectory. Experiments with Lorenz-96 and surface quasi-geostrophic (SQG) dynamics show a clear regime dependence. For linear observations, a well-tuned LETKF is more accurate, while CI-EnSF maintains stable cycling and effective covariance-mediated information propagation. Under strongly nonlinear observations and under climatological initialization, CI-EnSF achieves lower analysis error and greater cycling robustness than Gaussian ensemble benchmarks such as the LETKF, with improvements extending across spatial scales in the nonlinear SQG experiment. These results suggest that the principal benefit of CI-EnSF arises from combining nonlinear distributional transport with the mature covariance geometry used in conventional data assimilation.

item.title: HUST-Grace2026s: a high-resolution static gravity field product from GRACE and GRACE-FO observations (2002–2025)
item.dc:creator: Lijun Zheng, Hao Zhou, Xiang Guo, Zebing Zhou, Zhicai Luo
item.description:
Earth System Science Data — matched: ice sheet, climate change
By combining over twenty years of satellite data from the GRACE (Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment) and GRACE-FO (Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment Follow-on) missions, this research creates a unified and highly accurate map of Earth's gravity field. Our advanced processing technique significantly improves accuracy, reducing errors by over half compared to previous models. The resulting dataset is crucial for precisely tracking long-term environmental shifts, such as water storage changes and ice sheet melt, thereby improving our understanding of climate change impacts.

item.title: Data Quality Audit and Bivariate Temperature-Humidity Analysis of a Long-Term LoRaWAN Network: Anomaly Detection, PCA, Clustering and Machine Learning
item.dc:creator: Mamadou Sow
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: CO2, machine learning
arXiv:2610.32438v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Long-term environmental IoT/LPWAN deployments often aggregate heterogeneous data streams from diverse devices without systematic auditing of each variable's actual coverage prior to analysis-an increased risk when multiple sensor types coexist within the same network. This work proposes a C++17 processing pipeline applied to the Tour Perret LoRaWAN dataset (421 937 frames, June 2021--June 2023, 5 devices). A systematic coverage audit integrated into the extraction phase reveals that CO2 is completely missing (0% coverage) and pressure is reported only by an isolated base module (Wyres, 4.24% of the corpus), invalidating the initial hypothesis of a joint four-variable analysis. The analysis is refocused on the Temperature--Humidity pair, jointly available across 205{,}005 frames (95.76%) from 4 Elsys EMS sensors. The pipeline sequentially performs anomaly detection (modified Z-score, Isolation Forest), bivariate Principal Component Analysis, clustering (K-means, DBSCAN), and a multilayer perceptron predicting humidity from temperature and time, whose residuals serve as a detector for slow drift. On real-world data: Temperature--Humidity correlation r=-0.662, two-component PCA (PC1 =83.1% of variance), Isolation Forest detects 2.12% multivariate anomalies while univariate Z-score detects none, calibrated DBSCAN isolates 0.17% noise across 13 clusters, and the MLP achieves $R^2=0.672$ (RMSE =10.54%) in cross-validation. This work demonstrates that per-variable coverage auditing prior to modeling is a necessary methodological step for heterogeneous multi-sensor IoT datasets.

item.title: Probability indication maps for avalanche runout for decision support in daily traffic rout risk management
item.dc:creator: Julia Glaus, Jan Kleinn, Lukas Stoffel, Pia Ruttner, Katreen Wikstrom Jones, Johan Gaume, … (+1)
item.description:
The Cryosphere
Snow avalanches threaten roads, ski areas, and communities in mountain regions. We present a practical method to create daily maps showing where avalanches are likely to travel and how strong they may be. By combining weather data, snow measurements, and computer simulations, our approach supports safer decisions on road closures and avalanche control and helps protect people and infrastructure.

item.title: AstroComb(v.1.0): non-linear, multi-channel, probabilistic cyclostratigraphic analysis
item.dc:creator: Iris Fernandes, Klaus Mosegaard, Aske L. Sørensen, Mohammad Youssof, Nicolas Thibault, Tais W. Dahl
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
We introduce a new method to more precisely date ancient sediment layers using astronomical time cycles recorded in the rock. Unlike previous tools, it handles complex, multi-channel data without oversimplifying and gives clear estimates of dating uncertainty. This helps future research in better understand Earth's past climate, biological changes, and geologic events with greater confidence and accuracy.

item.title: Observation operator and detection limits for MODIS and VIIRS Fire Radiative Power products
item.dc:creator: Mikhail Sofiev, Rostislav Kouznetsov
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
Satellites can observe fires globally, but sensitivity of instruments in space is limited: they miss small fires and cannot see through clouds. We analyzed fire observations of two instruments and obtained their sensitivity to small fires, which depends on the resolution of the instrument, timing of the observation (day or night), and details of the data processing. We developed a procedure for comparing fire model predictions with satellite observations accounting for their limited sensitivity.
